newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strikes hit French air traffic, press, hospitals.
newsitem.headline: Strikes hit French air traffic, press, hospitals.

text.p: Strikes disrupted French air traffic and state hospitals on Thursday, and most newspapers failed to appear as printers joined in the labour unrest.
National newspapers were absent from newsstands while a few regional titles appeared as normal. Some dailies were available on the Internet computer network even if they did not make it onto paper.
The printers' branch of the Communist-led CGT union called the 24-hour strike to protest at cuts in state subsidies to the media, suppression of tax breaks and rising postal charges.
It also demanded retirement at 55 instead of at 60, a move the CGT says will help cut record 12.8 percent unemployment.
British Airways French units Air Liberte and TAT cut flights by half on the second day of a 48-hour strike by cockpit crew.
A company spokeswoman for the airlines said TAT, a domestic airline, would guarantee 91 of 180 scheduled flights.
Air Liberte, which flies around the world, would cancel 33 of its 60 flights but would operate all long-haul flights.
The stoppage is due to end at noon (1000 GMT) on Friday.
The strikers planned a protest march later in the day to the headquarters of Air Liberte at Paris' Orly airport.

Unions are protesting over pay and conditions which they say will be affected by a merger of the two airlines. Marc Rochet, chairman of the two units, has rejected demands for reforms which he said would raise costs by 18 percent.
Junior hospital doctors kept up a strike, now in its fifth week, although their representatives met aides of Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot overnight to discuss the dispute.
The strikers are protesting against government plans to fine doctors exceeding pre-set prescription targets, in order to curb health spending and plug the gaping welfare deficit.

The doctors' dispute, like demands for early retirement, are testing the conservative government's determination to cut public deficits to qualify for the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
